blocks.text: Displacement-time graphs are important tools in kinematics, because they provide a visual representation of an object's motion. Here's why we discuss them:

items: They give a clear picture of how an object's position changes over time.
They help us easily determine whether an object is moving, stationary or accelerating.

blocks.text: In a displacement-time graph, the displacement (\(x\)) is plotted on the \(y\)-axis, and time (\(t\)) is plotted on the \(x\)-axis.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Be careful with the letters: in kinematics \(x\) is the displacement, but on this graph it is drawn on the vertical axis (the usual \(y\)-axis), while time \(t\) runs along the horizontal axis. Each point \((t, x)\) of the graph tells you where the particle is at time \(t\).
Key Features of a Displacement-Time Graph
1. Slope of the graph \(= \left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)\), represents velocity of the particle.

If velocity is uniform i.e.,
\[v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = \text{Slope of the graph}\]
\[= \text{constant},\]
the displacement-time graph is a straight line.

items: If \(v = \frac{dx}{dt} = 0\), the particle is at rest and the displacement-time graph is a horizontal line, which reflects that displacement remains constant with time. In Figure 7.1, the particle is at rest from point \(B\) to point \(C\).

If \(v = \frac{dx}{dt} = \) constant \(> 0\), the particle moves forward, and the displacement-time graph is a rising straight line; that is, displacement increases as time increases. In Figure 7.1, the particle is moving with positive uniform velocity from point \(A\) to point \(B\).

If \(v = \frac{dx}{dt} = \) constant \(< 0\), the particle moves in the opposite direction, and the displacement time graph is a falling straight line; that is, displacement decreases as time increases. In Figure 7.1, the particle is moving with uniform negative velocity from point \(C\) to point \(D\).

blocks.alt: Displacement-time graph with x on the vertical axis and t on the horizontal axis. A straight segment rises from A at the origin to B (v greater than 0), a horizontal segment runs from B to C (v = 0), and a straight segment falls from C to D (v less than 0).
blocks.caption: Figure 7.1: displacement-time graph: rising from A to B, horizontal from B to C, falling from C to D (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Recall!
blocks.text:
Positive slope: forward motion.
Negative slope: backward motion.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is the slope the velocity? Between two points of the graph, slope \(= \frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\), which is exactly the average velocity (7.1.3). For a straight segment this ratio is the same everywhere, so the velocity is constant. If the graph is a curve, the velocity keeps changing, and the velocity at an instant is the slope of the tangent at that point, \(\frac{dx}{dt}\).
Reading a graph quickly: steeper means faster; horizontal means at rest; a falling segment means moving back towards (or past) the origin. The slope has units: km per minute, m per second, and so on, taken from the two axes.

blocks.alt: Grid graph of displacement x in km (0 to 7) against t in minutes (0 to 70). Straight line from O(0, 0) up to A(20, 4), horizontal to B(50, 4), then straight down to C(60, 0).
blocks.caption: Figure 7.2: displacement-time graph of the cyclist's journey (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Example 3
blocks.problem:
A cyclist rides in a straight line for 20 minutes. He then stops and waits for 30 minutes, after which he returns in a straight line to the starting point in 10 minutes. Figure 7.2 shows the displacement-time graph for his journey.
(a) Calculate the average velocity for each stage of the journey in km/h.
(b) Calculate the average velocity for the whole journey.
(c) Find the average speed for the whole journey.
steps:
Given: the graph of Figure 7.2 with the corner points \(O(0, 0)\), \(A(20, 4)\), \(B(50, 4)\), \(C(60, 0)\) (time in minutes, displacement in km).
To find: (a) average velocity on OA, AB and BC in km/h; (b) average velocity for the whole journey; (c) average speed for the whole journey.
Method: for each stage read the time taken and the change in displacement from the graph, then use average velocity = displacement / time. Change km/min to km/h by multiplying by 60 (1 h = 60 min).

(a) Journey from O to A
Time = 20 mins, displacement = 4 km.
\[\text{Average velocity} = \dfrac{\text{Displacment}}{\text{Time}}\]
\[= \dfrac{4}{20} = \dfrac{1}{5}\ \text{km/min}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{5} \times 60 = 12\ \text{km/h}\]
Why: on the graph, x goes from 0 to 4 while t goes from 0 to 20. In one hour he would cover 60 times what he covers in one minute.

Journey from A to B
Time = 30 mins, displacement = 0 km.
\[\text{Average velocity} = \dfrac{\text{Displacment}}{\text{Time}}\]
\[= \dfrac{0}{30} = 0\ \text{km/min}\]
\[= 0 \times 60 = 0\ \text{km/h}\]
\(\Rightarrow\) object is stationary.
Why: AB is horizontal; x stays 4 km, so the change in displacement is zero.

Journey from B to C
Time = 10 mins, displacement = \(-4\) km.
\[\text{Average velocity} = \dfrac{\text{Displacment}}{\text{Time}}\]
\[= \dfrac{-4}{10} = -\dfrac{2}{5}\ \text{km/min}\]
\[= -\dfrac{2}{5} \times 60 = -24\ \text{km/h}\]
Why: x falls from 4 to 0, so the change is \(0 - 4 = -4\) km. The minus sign says he is riding back towards the start.

(b) Whole journey
\[\text{Total displacement} = 4 + 0 + (-4) = 0\]
\[\text{Average velocity} = \dfrac{0}{60} = 0\]
Why: he ends where he started (C is on the t-axis), so the displacement for the whole journey is 0, and therefore the average velocity is also 0.

(c) Average speed for the whole journey
Total time = 60 mins = 1 h; Total distance = 4 + 4 = 8 km.
\[\text{Average speed} = \dfrac{\text{Total distance}}{\text{Total time}}\]
\[= \dfrac{8}{1}\ \text{km/h} = 8\ \text{km/h}\]
Why: distance counts both the 4 km out and the 4 km back, without signs. The waiting time is part of the journey, so it is included in the total time.

Check:
The stage velocities are the slopes of OA, AB and BC: \(\frac{4}{20} > 0\), \(0\), \(\frac{-4}{10} < 0\), matching rising, flat and falling segments. Also, displacement = velocity \(\times\) time on each stage: \(12 \times \frac{20}{60} + 0 + (-24) \times \frac{10}{60} = 4 - 4 = 0\) km, as in (b).
blocks.answer: (a) O to A: 12 km/h; A to B: 0 km/h (stationary); B to C: \(-24\) km/h. (b) 0 km/h. (c) 8 km/h.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the solution of Example 3 the book prints "Displacment" three times; it should be "Displacement". The book also prints a stray arrow mark before "\(0 \times 60 = 0\) km/h" in the journey from A to B; the line is simply \(0 \times 60 = 0\) km/h. The answers are not affected.

blocks.caption: Figure 7.3: displacement-time graph of Javed's journey, drawn with the kilometre values the book's solution uses (original drawing after the textbook's figure; see the Book correction)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Figure 7.3 in the book numbers its vertical axis 0 to 9 and labels it "Displacement (km)", so A appears at 6 km and C at 8 km. This cannot be right: the first drive is 2 h at 50 km/h, that is 100 km, and the book's own solution reads the axis as "6 units = 100 km". The axis numbers are grid units, not kilometres: A is at 100 km and C at \(\frac{400}{3} \approx 133.3\) km. The printed figure also puts the label O beside the axis value 2, although O is the origin. Our drawing shows the kilometre values the solution uses.

blocks.title: Example 4
blocks.problem:
Javed drives from his home to Murree. He drives for 2 hours at an average velocity of 50 km/h. He then stops for lunch before continuing to Murree. Figure 7.3 shows a displacement-time graph for his journey.
(a) Work out the displacement of Murree from Javed's home.
(b) Work out his average velocity for his whole journey.
steps:
Given: first drive O to A: 2 h at an average velocity of 50 km/h; lunch stop A to B (from \(t = 2\) h to \(t = 3\) h); second drive B to C (from \(t = 3\) h to \(t = 4\) h), as in Figure 7.3.
To find: (a) the displacement of Murree (point C) from home (point O); (b) the average velocity for the whole journey.
Method: the first drive gives the displacement at A from displacement = average velocity \(\times\) time. That known value fixes the scale of the vertical axis, and the scale gives the rise from B to C. Then average velocity = total displacement / total time.

(a) Journey from O to A
Time = 2 h; average velocity = 50 km/h.
\[\text{average velocity} = \dfrac{\text{Displacement}}{\text{Time}}\]
\[50 = \dfrac{\text{Displacement}}{2}\]
\[\text{Displacement} = 50 \times 2 = 100\ \text{km}\]
Why: the definition of average velocity, solved for the displacement.

Scale on vertical axis from graph
\[6\ \text{units} = 100\ \text{km}\]
\[1\ \text{unit} = \dfrac{100}{6} = \dfrac{50}{3}\ \text{km}\]
Why: on the book's printed grid, A stands 6 squares (units) above the time axis, and we have just found that the displacement at A is 100 km. (See the Book correction above: the printed axis counts these grid units although it is labelled km. On our redrawn Figure 7.3 the values are already in km.)

Journey from B to C
\[\text{vertical rise} = 2\ \text{units}\]
\[\text{Displacement} = 2 \times \dfrac{50}{3}\]
\[= \dfrac{100}{3}\ \text{km}\]
Why: on the printed grid C is 2 units higher than B (8 units against 6), and each unit is \(\frac{50}{3}\) km.

Total displacement
\[100 + \dfrac{100}{3} = \dfrac{400}{3}\]
\[\approx 133.3\ \text{km}\]
Why: the lunch stop adds nothing (AB is horizontal), so the total is the first drive plus the second drive. This is the displacement of Murree from Javed's home.

(b) Average velocity
Time = 2 h (first drive) + 1 h (lunch stop) + 1 h (second drive) = 4 h.
Total displacement = 133.3 km.
\[\text{Average velocity} = \dfrac{133.3}{4}\]
\[\approx 33.33\ \text{km/h}\]
Why: the lunch hour is part of the journey, so it is counted in the total time. Exactly: \(\frac{400/3}{4} = \frac{100}{3} \approx 33.33\) km/h.

Check:
On the redrawn Figure 7.3 the point C is \((4, 133.3)\); the average velocity is the slope of the straight line from O to C: \(\frac{133.3 - 0}{4 - 0} \approx 33.33\). It is less than 50 km/h, as it must be, because the lunch hour (velocity 0) and the slower second drive (\(\frac{100}{3}\) km in 1 h) pull the average down.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Displacement \(x\) goes on the vertical axis and time \(t\) on the horizontal axis.
2. Slope of a displacement-time graph \(= \frac{dx}{dt} =\) velocity.
3. Straight line: uniform velocity. Rising: \(v > 0\) (forward); horizontal: \(v = 0\) (at rest); falling: \(v < 0\) (backward).
4. Average velocity over an interval = change in \(x\) / change in \(t\) = slope of the chord joining the two points.
5. Waiting time counts in the total time of a journey.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Reading a falling line as "slowing down". A falling straight line means constant negative velocity (moving back), not decreasing speed.
2. Reading a horizontal line as "moving at constant speed". Horizontal on a displacement-time graph means at rest.
3. Leaving out the stop when finding the total time (in Example 4 the total time is 4 h, not 3 h).
4. Forgetting the units: dividing km by minutes gives km/min; multiply by 60 to get km/h.
